notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Deuteronomy 23, drawn from the sources I could access. (Search and fetch limits prevented me from reaching Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox, and modern-scholarship pages directly; where those traditions have well-known distinctive readings, I have noted what the available commentaries report about them.)

---

## Verses 1–8: Exclusion from the Assembly

**v. 1 — “No man with crushed or severed genitals may enter the assembly of the LORD.”**

The Hebrew describes two conditions: “bruised by crushing” (testicles) and “cut off with respect to the penis” — i.e., a eunuch by birth defect, accident, or deliberate castration (Precept Austin cites NET notes and Utley). The key debate is what “assembly of the LORD” (*qahal*) means. Several older commentators (Gill, Poole, Trapp, Clarke) argue it refers to **civil leadership** — the elders, judges, and rulers of Israel — not to participation in worship or the covenant community. Gill writes: “by the congregation is to be understood the elders, judges, and representatives of the people, that met together … to execute judgment” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm). Guzik (Enduring Word) likewise leans toward this political-leadership reading, noting that Deuteronomy 31:28–30 uses “congregation” for elders and officers (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-23/).  

Others hold that “assembly of the LORD” means the gathered worship community at the tabernacle/temple (Precept Austin cites MacArthur, the HCSB Study Bible, and Utley). The NET notes suggest the prohibition may be “primarily polemical” — sexually damaged persons were associated with pagan temple personnel, so Israel was to make a clean break from Canaanite practice (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-23-commentary).  

The reason for exclusion, regardless of the assembly’s precise nature, is tied to the covenant’s connection with “seed” and wholeness. Isaiah 56:3–5 and Acts 8:26–40 show that under the new covenant, eunuchs are fully welcomed (Guzik; Precept Austin).

URLs: enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-23/ ; preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-23-commentary ; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm

---

**v. 2 — “No one of illegitimate birth may enter the assembly of the LORD, nor any of his descendants, even to the tenth generation.”**

The Hebrew word *mamzer* is difficult. The LXX translates it “one born of a harlot,” but most Hebrew scholars narrow it to a child of **incestuous union** (the dominant view in the Talmud and among commentators like Utley, Deere, and the Believer’s Study Bible — see preceptaustin.org). Others say it could mean a child of mixed marriage between an Israelite and a pagan (cf. Nehemiah 13:23). Guzik notes that “some later Jewish writers defined this as someone who was born of an incestuous relationship between Jews; others said it refers to those born of mixed marriages” (enduringword.com).  

“To the tenth generation” is idiomatic for **permanence** or “as long as the nation exists” (Kalland, cited by Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics calls it “a periphrasis for ‘forever’” (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/23.htm). The purpose was to place an indelible stigma on shameful sexual misconduct (MacArthur, cited by Precept Austin).  

The Pulpit Commentary notes that “the outward bar no longer exists, and the offspring of impure connection, if children of faith, are welcomed to the spiritual fold,” but warns that parents who sin themselves out of church fellowship do their children irreparable harm (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/23.htm).

---

**vv. 3–6 — Ammonites and Moabites excluded forever.**

Two reasons are given in v. 4: (1) they did not meet Israel with bread and water on the way out of Egypt, and (2) they hired Balaam to curse Israel. Gill notes that the first charge (inhospitality) falls on the Ammonites and the second (Balaam) on the Moabites (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm). Behind this lies the disgraceful origin of both peoples — born from Lot’s incest with his daughters (Genesis 19:30–38), which ties back to the concern in v. 2 about incestuous origins (Precept Austin; Guzik).  

Verse 5 stresses that God turned Balaam’s intended curse into a blessing **because the LORD your God loves you** — a theme that runs through Deuteronomy (4:37; 7:7–8; 10:15; 33:3). Utley at Bible.org emphasizes that YHWH’s actions are based on His elective choice, not Israel’s goodness (bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-23).  

Verse 6 — “You are not to seek their peace or prosperity” — means no treaties, alliances, or prayers for their national welfare (Utley notes this may refer to treaties per Ezra 9:12 or prayers per Jeremiah 14:11). It does not forbid personal kindness (Gill cites David’s kindness to Hanun the Ammonite in 2 Samuel 10:2 as proof).  

**Ruth the Moabitess** is the classic example showing these national bans did not bar individuals from joining the covenant community. Merrill (cited by Guzik) says: “Disbarment from the assembly was not synonymous with exclusion from the covenant community itself as the one example of Ruth the Moabite makes clear.” The Jewish tradition (Rashi, cited by Ellicott) held that the ban applied only to Moabite and Ammonite **men**, not women — “the children, according to Jewish law, follow the father, not the mother” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/23.htm). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary agrees: “This was a national curse, and applied to the nations as such. It did not apply to individuals” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-23.html).

---

**vv. 7–8 — Edomites and Egyptians: a different standard.**

Edomites are called “your brother” because Esau was Jacob’s twin (Genesis 25:24–26; 36:1). Egyptians are shown favour because Israel “lived as a foreigner in his land” — a reminder of early hospitality before the oppression began. The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics observes: “Past kindnesses are not to be forgotten because of a late change of disposition. The Egyptians were kindly remembered, though their treatment of the Israelites had latterly been very cruel” (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/23.htm).  

The practical difference: Edomites and Egyptians could enter the assembly in the **third generation**, presumably the time needed for full integration into Israel’s society and worship (Utley, bible.org). Gill explains that the third generation is counted from the time any Edomite or Egyptian became a proselyte — their grandchildren could be full members (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm).  

Kline (cited by Coffman) notes that the different treatment of Edomites/Egyptians versus Moabites/Ammonites proves the exclusions were not primarily racial or ethnic: “Mercy and morality were the vital principles of covenant administration” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/deuteronomy-23.html).

---

## Verses 9–14: Purity of the Military Camp

**v. 9 — “When you are encamped against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every wicked thing.”**

This introduces a section on ceremonial and physical cleanliness during “holy war.” Rashi (cited by Ellicott) says: “Because Satan maketh his accusations in the hour of danger” — spiritual vigilance is most needed when facing battle. Utley explains that YHWH fought for Israel, but they had to remain ceremonially pure for His presence to remain with them (bible.org). Gill adds that soldiers facing death should be especially careful about sin, yet “how little are these things thought of by such in common!” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm).

---

**vv. 10–11 — Nocturnal emission.**

The “occurrence in the night” (literally “a happening at night”) refers primarily to involuntary seminal emission, though Utley notes it could include other bodily discharges (urination, diarrhea — bible.org). The man must leave camp, wash at evening, and return after sunset. This is ceremonial, not moral, uncleanness — following the pattern of Leviticus 15:16–18. Guzik observes: “Though the passage in no way suggests that bodily emissions … are in themselves inherently evil or even cultically impure, it does underscore the importance of a proper time and place for such things” (quoting Merrill, enduringword.com).

---

**vv. 12–14 — Sanitary provisions.**

A designated latrine area outside the camp and a digging tool (“paddle” or “spade” — Hebrew term uncertain, possibly a tent peg or a weapon used for double duty) were required. Excrement had to be buried. Gill lists reasons: “to preserve modesty and decency … cleanliness in the camp, and the health of themselves and their fellow soldiers” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary says: “This requirement was for both natural and spiritual reasons: to provide a sanitary camp site; and to provide a place ceremonially clean for the Presence of Jehovah God to be among them” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-23.html).  

Verse 14 gives the theological foundation: **“For the LORD your God walks throughout your camp.”** Spurgeon preached on this verse, noting God’s presence was not confined to the tabernacle: “No part of the camp was exempt from God’s walking in it. Not merely in the holy place was God … but he was everywhere in the streets of the canvas city, and in the outskirts thereof” (cited by Guzik, enduringword.com). Meyer adds: “God is ever patrolling the avenues of our life. The most secret processes of our daily existence … the thoughts and intents of our heart, are all manifest to Him.” The warning is stark: if God sees “anything indecent” (*ervat dabar*, literally “nakedness of a thing”), He may **turn away** — withdraw His protective presence, leading to military defeat (Guzik; Precept Austin).

---

## Verses 15–16: The Escaped Slave

**v. 15 — “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you.”**

The consensus among commentators is that this refers to a **foreign slave** escaping a foreign master (not an Israelite slave from an Israelite master, which would conflict with other laws). Thompson (cited by Guzik): “The refugee slave referred to had evidently come from a foreign land. Otherwise there would have been legal complications” (enduringword.com). Morgan: “Israel was to be a refuge for the oppressed slaves of other people.”  

Utley at Bible.org highlights how radical this was: “All other ancient Near Eastern law codes demanded the return (and with it probable death) of runaway slaves. The Mosaic covenant focuses on the rights and protection of the weak, powerless, socially ostracized, and poor” (bible.org). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary specifies such a slave “had fled from a foreign master to escape his harsh treatment” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-23.html).  

**v. 16** grants the escaped slave full freedom: live wherever he chooses, in whatever town pleases him, without oppression. Gill says: “he was not to be detained … or be obliged to dwell in any certain place under restraint” but could choose whatever was “most for his good, profit, and advantage” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/23.htm).

---

## Verses 17–18: Sacred Prostitution Banned

**v. 17 — “No daughter or son of Israel is to be a shrine prostitute.”**

The Hebrew terms are *qedeshah* (feminine “holy one”) and *qadesh* (masculine “holy one”) — used ironically for cult prostitutes. Canaanite fertility religions employed ritual sex to induce the gods to release procreative power. Guzik notes: “Whole guilds of male and female temple personnel participated in grossly sexual rituals … Nowhere was this more commonly practiced than among the peoples of Syria and Canaan” (quoting Merrill, enduringword.com). The Bridgeway Commentary explains: “Prostitution was regarded among many ancient heathen nations as an act of religious worship” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/deuteronomy-23.html).  

**v. 18 — “You must not bring the wages of a prostitute … into the house of the LORD your God.”**

“The wages of a dog” refers to the pay of a male prostitute — “dog” (*kelev*) was a term for a male cult prostitute in the ancient Near East (Thompson, cited by Guzik). Goliath’s “Am I a dog?” (1 Samuel 17:43) and Paul’s “Beware of dogs” (Philippians 3:2) may carry this connotation (Guzik). The point is that God rejects revenue from sexual sin, even when offered as a vow. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary states: “Both males and females prostituted themselves in the service of the goddess Astarte. All such practices were abomination in Israel” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/deuteronomy-23.html).  

Utley notes some scholarly debate about whether vv. 17–18 refer specifically to cultic prostitution or also to common prostitution; the parallelism suggests both are in view (bible.org).

---

## Verses 19–20: Interest on Loans

**v. 19 — “Do not charge your brother interest on money, food, or any other type of loan.”**

The Hebrew *neshek* comes from a root meaning “to bite” — hence “biting interest” or usury. Guzik: “The mention of food, and the similar command in Exodus 22:25, leads most to understand that interest was prohibited on loans made to the poor for their basic needs, and did not prohibit the taking of interest on loans that were not for relief of the poor” (enduringword.com). Merrill (cited by Guzik) notes: “To exact penalties of a brother is to put the ‘bite’ on him.” Thompson adds that ancient Near Eastern interest rates were exorbitant — some Nuzi contracts show rates of 50% (enduringword.com).  

**v. 20 — “You may charge a foreigner interest.”**  

The distinction rests on the nature of the loan: loans to a foreigner were typically commercial/mercantile, while loans to a brother were for relief of poverty. Kalland (cited by Guzik): “But since merchants from other nations might come for business reasons to Israel … foreigners could be charged interest.” The purpose clause — “so that the LORD your God may bless you” — ties covenant obedience to divine blessing. Utley notes: “Several of these ‘blessing texts’ occur in the context of Israel helping the poor and needy (e.g., 14:29; 24:19)” (bible.org).

---

## Verses 21–23: Keeping Vows

**v. 21 — “If you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to keep it.”**

Vows are voluntary promises made to God, but once made they are binding. The Hebrew construction “will surely require it” is emphatic (infinitive absolute + imperfect verb), meaning God takes the matter with utmost seriousness (Utley, bible.org). Guzik says: “Breaking a vow is treated as stealing from God Himself” (enduringword.com). The rabbis later interpreted “do not delay” as meaning no longer than three festivals, i.e., one year (Utley).  

**v. 22 — “But if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin.”**  

Vows are never required. It is often wiser not to vow at all. Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 echoes this: “Better not to vow than to vow and not pay.”  

**v. 23 — “Be careful to follow through on what comes from your lips.”**  

The spoken word carried immense weight in Hebrew thought. Guzik addresses the New Testament question about oaths (Matthew 5:34–37; James 5:12), arguing that Jesus was not forbidding all oaths but teaching that integrity should make oaths unnecessary — Jesus Himself answered under oath in court (Matthew 26:63–64), and God swears oaths (Luke 1:73; Hebrews 6:13, 17) (enduringword.com).  

The Pulpit Commentary notes: “A vow to the Lord, once made, was to be religiously kept; the Lord would require it, and to refuse or neglect to pay it would be held a sin. No one, however, was under any obligation to vow—that was to be a purely voluntary act” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-23.html).

---

## Verses 24–25: Gleaning Rights for the Traveller

**v. 24 — “When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes, but you must not put any in your basket.”**  

**v. 25 — “When you enter your neighbor’s grainfield, you may pluck the heads of grain with your hand, but you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain.”**  

This was a provision for immediate hunger, not a harvesting right. Guzik explains: “It wasn’t the right to harvest from your neighbor’s fields, but to provide for your own immediate needs” (enduringword.com). Utley highlights the generosity: the phrase “until you are fully satisfied” combines “according to your desire” and “your fill” — “It speaks, not of eating enough just to get by, but of eating all you want. What a marvelous provision for the poor, needy, and alien passing by” (bible.org).  

This is the law Jesus and His disciples operated under when they plucked grain on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1–8; Mark 2:23–28; Luke 6:1–5). The Pharisees accused them of Sabbath-breaking, not theft — they knew this Deuteronomy provision (Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary adds that among Arabs of the 19th century, “the right of a hungry person to pluck ears of corn in a field and eat the grains is still recognized” (Robinson and Thomson, cited in studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-23.html).  

Kalland (cited by Guzik) warns: “On the other hand, this advantage was not to be abused by putting grapes in a basket or putting a sickle to the neighbor’s grain for one’s future use.”

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources I could access reveal several points of divergence:

**1. Meaning of “assembly of the LORD” (vv. 1–8):**  
- **Older Reformed/Anglican commentators** (Gill, Poole, Trapp, Clarke) and **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic)** read it as civil leadership — elders and rulers.  
- **Dispensational-leaning evangelical** (MacArthur, Deere in Bible Knowledge Commentary) and **broader evangelical** (Utley, NET notes) read it as the gathered worship assembly at the tabernacle.  
- The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (representing a **broader Protestant homiletic tradition**) takes a mediating view — “the congregation does not always signify the sum total of the people, but the great assembly of elders” — i.e., office-holders in the theocracy (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/23.htm).

**2. Usury/Interest (vv. 19–20):**  
The traditional **Reformed** and **Baptist** reading (seen in Gill, Guzik, and the Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary) is that the prohibition applies specifically to loans to the poor for subsistence, not commercial loans. The Hebrew *neshek* (“biting”) is understood as excessive or oppressive interest. This differs from the historic **Catholic** position, which for centuries prohibited all interest on loans (usury) based partly on this passage — though I was unable to access Catholic sources to document this directly.

**3. Vows and Oaths (vv. 21–23):**  
Some **Anabaptist and Quaker** traditions have historically taken Jesus’ words in Matthew 5:34–37 as an absolute prohibition of all oaths, including in court. The majority **Reformed, Lutheran, and evangelical** view (reflected in Guzik) holds that Jesus was prohibiting flippant or deceptive oaths, not all oath-taking, since God Himself swears oaths and Jesus answered under oath. I was unable to access specific Lutheran, Methodist, or Anabaptist pages to compare.

**4. The Escaped Slave (vv. 15–16):**  
The unanimous evangelical reading sees this as referring to foreign slaves. This interpretation partly arose to reconcile this law with passages that regulate Israelite slavery. The **19th-century American debate** over slavery saw some pro-slavery interpreters argue this only applied to slaves fleeing pagan masters, while abolitionists saw a broader humanitarian principle — though I did not find this directly discussed in the sources accessed.

---

## Other Views (Limited by Access)

I was unable to fetch pages from **newadvent.org** (Catholic), **catholic.com**, **oca.org** (Orthodox), **bibleodyssey.org**, or **netbible.org** directly due to search/fetch limits. However, Precept Austin does cite the NET Bible notes at several points (see notes on vv. 1, 2, 3 above). The NET notes tend to emphasize the polemical/Canaanite-background reading of the exclusions and clarify that the Hebrew *qahal* refers to formal tabernacle/temple services rather than the nation as a whole.

The Precept Austin compilation also notes the Septuagint’s translation of *qahal* as *ekklesia* — the very word the New Testament uses for “church” — which is a significant connection in **Orthodox** and **Catholic** ecclesiology (the Church as the continuation and fulfillment of the OT assembly), though I could not verify how those traditions specifically exposit this chapter.
